Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE); Luis Ortega (Redwood SE); Aisha Rahman (Head of ML, Harbor Fintech); Ben Carter (Platform Engineer); Jon Park (CTO)

summary: Discovery focused on model selection tradeoffs across Hosted, Dedicated and Private for Harbor Fintech. Main questions: context length needs (8k vs 32k vs 65k), multilingual support, tool/function-calling (external API calls, retrieval), latency vs cost tradeoffs, and security/compliance requirements for production. Agreed next steps: benchmarks on customer prompts, pricing comparison, and share security docs.
topics: Introductions; Current stack and constraints; Context length and latency requirements; Open model comparisons (LLaMA variants, Mistral, Orca-like, Falcon); Quantization and cost; Multilingual and tokenization; Tool-calling / function-calling support; Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs; Security and compliance; Next steps & action items
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, our account lead. Luis is our solutions engineer. Could you all do quick intros?
[00:12] Aisha (Harbor): Hi, I'm Aisha, Head of ML at Harbor Fintech. We're building doc understanding + customer reply automation across 6 languages.
[00:20] Ben (Harbor): Ben here, platform eng, looking after infra and latency SLAs.
[00:25] Jon (Harbor): Jon, CTO, interested in cost predictability and data residency.
[00:32] Luis (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Quick agenda — model selection, context length, multilingual, tool-calling, and deployment options (Hosted/Dedicated/Private).
[00:45] Aisha: Our main constraints — some workflows need 8k context, a subset needs 32k for long statements and attachments. We also have multi-lingual traffic: EN, ES, PT, FR, and occasionally JP. Latency target for interactive flows is ~300-500ms per request 95p, but for async batch it's looser.
[01:08] Ben: Also we need audit logs and KMS for keys; SOC2 is mandatory. We may require VPC or on-prem for a subset of PII processing.
[01:22] Luis: Understood. For context lengths, are you thinking single input documents or retrieval-augmented pipelines?
[01:28] Aisha: Mostly RAG — we pull in customer history and document chunks, so effective token windows can hit 20k–30k when you include convo + docs.
[01:36] Maya: Ok. On model choices, we generally recommend evaluating a short-list of open models: LLaMA 2/3 variants (quantized), Mistral, Falcon, and some smaller instruction-tuned forks. There's also performance differences across context length and quantization.
[01:52] Jon: We care about hallucination for financial data — ability to do tool-calling to verify facts would help. Does Redwood support function calling / tool execution patterns?
[02:02] Luis: Yes — we support structured output and function/tool calling in the hosted API, and the same surface in Dedicated/Private. You can define functions and the runtime will stream a structured call. There are nuances with third-party tools and security — e.g., allowing outbound webhooks from Private requires network config.
[02:20] Ben: That network bit is critical. For Private we need explicit egress controls.
[02:26] Luis: Totally. In Private (VPC/on-prem) customers control egress and can add proxies or restricted routes.
[02:33] Aisha: For multilingual — tokenization affects cost and latency. Are there recommended models for non-English?
[02:40] Maya: Mistral and some LLaMA 3 checkpoints show good multilingual; Falcon sometimes lags on non-Latin scripts. We can share evals. Also quantization and instruction-tuning matter for safety and hallucination.
[02:55] Jon: Can you run a bench with our actual prompts? Synthetic numbers are helpful but real prompts are better.
[03:01] Luis: Absolutely. If you can share representative prompts and a few documents we can run throughput and latency tests for 8k/32k windows and give cost per-1000-tokens estimates.
[03:12] Aisha: We'll share 5 prompt sets and a mix of languages.
[03:18] Maya: On Hosted vs Dedicated: Hosted is quickest to start, pay-as-you-go, and we manage infra. Dedicated gives predictable throughput, reserved GPU pools, and better tail-latency for steady workloads. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for stricter data controls and compliance.
[03:36] Ben: For Dedicated, how flexible is autoscaling and burst? We might have spiky load.
[03:41] Luis: Dedicated has configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. You can set policies by route or model. If capacity is exhausted we have policy-based fallbacks to smaller models or different regions.
[03:52] Aisha: How about model variants for cost/latency tradeoffs — like using a 7B for routing quick replies and a 70B for confirmation?
[04:00] Luis: Yes, smart routing is supported. You can route by latency SLO, cost target, or content type. We also support prefix caching and KV caches for repeated context which cuts token costs.
[04:12] Jon: Are there differences in model availability across Hosted vs Private?
[04:16] Maya: Some experimental builds or curated models may be hosted-only initially, but we have a model catalog and can work on bringing variants to Dedicated/Private with validations.
[04:25] Ben: Security — we need SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC, audit trails, and KMS. Also retention controls and the ability to disable data retention on requests.
[04:36] Luis: We have SAML SSO, RBAC, request-level audit logs, and KMS integration. For Hosted we offer customer-managed encryption keys on some plans; Private gives full control.
[04:45] Aisha: What's tricky for us is the 32k+ effective context when you include retrieved docs. We need to understand tokenization and memory/kv cache behavior for long contexts.
[04:57] Luis: The runtime uses streaming KV cache, and the kernel selection will change for long sequences. For >32k we recommend models with tuned attention kernels; we can benchmark yours. Quantization also impacts memory and latency — int8 vs int4 tradeoffs are real.
[05:12] Aisha: Do you have multilingual QA evals? We need reliability across ES/PT/FR and some CJK.
[05:18] Maya: We'll share cross-lingual eval snapshots and per-token cost comparisons. Some models are better on Latin scripts. We can run your samples to measure exact quality metrics.
[05:28] Jon: Tool calling: can we restrict which functions can be invoked in production? We want fine-grained controls in case of untrusted prompts.
[05:35] Luis: Yes, you can whitelist functions per route and apply sandboxing for runtime connectors. Also we can log calls for audit.
[05:44] Ben: On observability — can we get per-token latency breakdowns and per-route dashboards?
[05:50] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost/latency and per-route dashboards with traces and errors. We can export to your monitoring stack.
[06:00] Aisha: Cost math — do you provide recommendations around batching and quantization for our workload? We currently have ~20M tokens/month and expect growth.
[06:08] Luis: Redwood Optimize suggests batching and quantization profiles. We'll suggest a profile for your mix of interactive vs batch flows. Batching lowers unit cost but can increase latency for single requests; we can simulate your QPS.
[06:22] Jon: Timeline — we're looking to pilot in Q3, production Q4. Security review and procurement will happen in parallel.
[06:29] Maya: Sounds reasonable. We'll prioritize a benchmark for your pilot cohort and send security docs.
[06:35] Ben: One more — data residency. Some EU customers require data never leave region. Hosted can be regionally isolated?
[06:42] Maya: Yes, hosted offers regional endpoints; Dedicated and Private give stronger guarantees. For strict residency, Private (on-prem or VPC) is the path.
[06:50] Aisha: Ok, let's go through a quick hypothetical: customer uploads a 20-page statement and wants a summarized action list across languages plus a verification call to an internal API.
[06:59] Luis: You'd likely do retrieval to extract chunks, pass through a 32k-capable model or chunk/summarize pipeline, then perform a tool/function call to your verification API. We can pipeline this with Redwood's streaming structured outputs so UX shows progress and fallback if verification fails.
[07:19] Jon: Fallbacks — how reliable are automatic fallbacks? If a large model is slow, can you degrade to smaller model gracefully without breaking semantics?
[07:27] Luis: We have A/B and canary controls, plus fallback policies that can switch model variant or region. There is some risk with smaller models changing output distribution; that's why we recommend eval sets and regression monitoring.
[07:40] Aisha: Can Redwood host our private checkpoints? We have internally-tuned models that we might want to run in Private.
[07:47] Maya: Yes, Private supports customer-supplied checkpoints with validation steps; Dedicated can sometimes host them under contract. We'll flag that for technical deep dive.
[07:56] Ben: Any constraints on third-party hardware (e.g., specific GPU types) for Dedicated?
[08:01] Luis: We operate across common GPU families; specific hardware can be arranged under Dedicated contracts but may affect pricing and availability.
[08:08] Jon: For procurement — what does pilot pricing look like? We want reserved baseline plus overage; also how does the SLA scale during pilot?
[08:16] Maya: For pilots we offer small dedicated capacity or hosted with usage credits depending on the commitment. We'll send a pricing sheet with reserved/dedicated pilot options.
[08:25] Aisha: Regarding evals, we want hallucination/regression checks for financial entities. Can Redwood tie eval alerts to model rollouts?
[08:33] Luis: Yes. Redwood Optimize has quality monitoring; you can attach prompt sets and get regression alerts tied to rollouts, and automatic rollback.
[08:42] Maya: Quick recap — Redwood will: 1) Run customer prompt benchmarks (Luis), 2) Send Hosted vs Dedicated pricing and pilot options (Maya), 3) Share security pack (SOC2/ISO/KMS) and region/residency info, 4) Schedule follow-up technical deep dive for Private/checkpoint ingestion if benchmarks look good.
[09:02] Jon: Sounds good. Any immediate blockers?
[09:05] Aisha: Just that we need the benchmark to see latency and hallucination numbers.
[09:09] Maya: We'll prioritize that.
[09:12] Ben: Thanks, we'll upload prompts and sample doc set to the secure drop.
[09:18] Luis: Great, once we have them we'll start runs and share CSVs and dashboards.
[09:23] Maya: Ok we'll follow up before EOD tomorrow with calendar invites for the deeper technical session.
[09:28] Jon: Thanks everybody.
[47:30] [end] Note: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings; some product names appear slightly off in the transcript (e.g., 'Llama' spelled as 'Llama'/"LLaMA", 'Mistral' pronounced 'Mistraal' once).
